vignette:
He is a 25-year-old Latin American man who comes to therapy carrying a kind of exhaustion that feels older than his years. By the time he first speaks about what happened, he has already learned to describe himself as "fine" in the way people do when they have gotten used to functioning while strained. He is single, lives alone, and works as a data scientist, a job he once enjoyed for its structure and logic. Lately, though, even the neatness of code and the predictability of numbers feel distant from the chaos that entered his life a little over a year ago.

The traumatic period begins with a phone call in the middle of an ordinary workday. His younger child, a toddler, has become suddenly and gravely ill. At first it sounds like the kind of emergency that resolves itself after a visit to urgent care, but within hours the family is in the hospital, and within days his world becomes measured in monitors, medications, and whispered updates from physicians. He remembers the smell of antiseptic, the brightness of the pediatric unit, and the way his own body seemed to vanish into a state of permanent alert. He sits beside the crib for hours, watching for every shift in breathing, every change in color, every glance between nurses that might signal disaster. He says that before this he believed he knew what love was; afterward, love becomes terror with no place to go.

The illness becomes life-threatening, and he lives in a kind of suspended time. He stops sleeping in any meaningful way. Even when he returns home, he lies awake listening for imagined alarms, replaying the last moments before the hospitalization, searching for what he could have done differently. His mind latches onto details with painful precision: the doctor's tone when explaining risks, the tiny pulse oximeter on the child's foot, the silence that follows bad news. He starts checking his phone obsessively, afraid to miss a call from the hospital. When he is at work, he stares at lines of data and realizes he is reading the same entry over and over without taking anything in. He continues to perform, at least outwardly, but colleagues begin to notice that he seems distracted, flat, and harder to reach.

Even after the child survives, the fear does not leave. In some ways, that is what surprises him most. He had expected relief to arrive all at once, but instead he finds himself jumping at the sound of a ringtone, scanning the child's face for signs of decline, and bracing for bad news whenever a routine appointment is scheduled. He avoids medical dramas on television and cannot sit through hospital scenes without feeling his chest tighten. He also avoids talking about the experience with most people because he does not want pity, and because once he starts describing it he feels the panic return in his body, hot and immediate. He says that people tell him he should feel grateful now, and he does, but gratitude and dread seem to live side by side, each one making the other more unbearable.

He notices that his relationships have become thinner. As a single man, he is used to privacy and self-reliance, but now the privacy feels more like isolation. He cancels plans, forgets to answer messages, and withdraws when friends ask how he is doing. He wants to be understood without having to explain the full story, yet he also feels embarrassed by how much the event still affects him. He does not cry easily, but he becomes tearful when he talks about the helplessness of standing beside a child he could not protect. That helplessness lingers in his body as tension in his shoulders, a tight jaw, and a constant readiness to move toward danger before it can fully arrive.

Over time, he begins to notice that his days are organized around prevention. He double-checks everything: appointments, medication schedules, the child's temperature when there is even a slight change in mood. At work, he becomes increasingly reliant on routines and written notes, because his concentration slips whenever he is tired or worried. He can still think abstractly and solve problems, but it takes more effort, and he is frustrated by how much mental energy now goes into simply keeping himself steady. He tells the story carefully, as if precision might keep it from overwhelming him, yet underneath the careful language is a man who is still living in the aftermath of a frightening period in which his child's life seemed precarious and his own sense of safety was permanently altered.
